By the second Saturday, they had a routine, and the routine was this: Tobias cast off, Wren took the wheel, and the two of them did not discuss their father.

The sunset cruise sold out. It turned out that what Saltmarsh Reach had wanted for forty years, without knowing it, was to sit on the open deck of the *Margaret Ann* with a paper cup of Prue's chowder and watch the sun go down behind Gullet Light. Wren had priced the tickets at twelve dollars. By the third cruise she raised them to fifteen, and nobody blinked.

Tobias was better with passengers than she was. He told them lies about the lighthouse, gorgeous elaborate lies about a keeper's daughter and a shipwrecked Portuguese sailor, and the tourists believed every word, and the locals laughed and corrected him, and both kinds of people tipped. He knew which island kids needed to be lifted down to the dock and which would be insulted. He remembered everyone's name, even people he hadn't seen since high school.

"You used to hate this," Wren said, when the passengers had gone ashore and he was hosing chowder off the benches. "You said the ferry was a prison that floated."

"I was nineteen. Everything was a prison." He coiled the hose. "Turns out the rest of the world is mostly parking lots."

"What did you do down there? In Baltimore."

"Tugs, for a while. Then a marine supply warehouse. Then a different warehouse." He shrugged. "Nothing worth putting in a ledger."

She watched him in the lavender light: the beard, the careful way he moved, as though something in his back had once been broken and set wrong. She wanted to ask about that. She wanted to ask about the fight, ten years ago, the one that had ended with their father throwing Toby's duffel off the end of the pier and Toby diving in after it in his clothes and swimming to the town dock and never coming back. She wanted to ask why he hadn't come to the funeral, and what he had been doing when he got her message, and whether he had cried.

Instead she said, "We cleared nine hundred tonight."

"Is that good?"

"It's good. It's not enough." She took the cash box into the wheelhouse and counted it again under the chart light, because counting things was what she did instead of feeling them. "Pell's note is a hundred and twenty. With the cruises and the charters and the skiff, I think we can get to maybe seventy by the end of June. Maybe."

Tobias leaned in the doorway. "And the other fifty?"

"I'm working on it."

"You're working on a calculator with a broken seven key." He'd noticed that. Of course he'd noticed that. "What about the house?"

"If I sell the house, where do I live?"

"With me," he said. "On the boat. Like pirates." And for one second he grinned at her, the old grin, the one from when she was eight and he was twelve and they used to steal the skiff to row out to the sandbar, and her chest hurt so badly she had to look down at the cash box.

They walked home together along Front Street, past the dark windows of the hardware store and the yellow window of the Anchor, where somebody was playing the jukebox. At the corner of Kettle Lane, Tobias stopped.

"Wren. About Dad."

She waited.

He shook his head. "Not tonight. Soon, though." He went up the walk ahead of her, and she heard him open the door to his old room for the first time in ten years, and she heard him stand there in the doorway a long time before he went in.
